utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Dimitrov. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dimitrov. Mr. Dimitrov do you recall that yesterday I show you first an extract from the first guest book, actually an extract that you provided to the Defence, and I indicated to you that there was a method of registering the guests which was that if one guest stayed seven days that guest will be registered every single day. Do you recall that, Mr. Dimitrov?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Then I show you an extract from the second guest book, which was 65 ter 1213, and I indicated to you that the method of recording changed with the second guest book, meaning that there will be a single entry per guest with the date and time of entry and then the date of departure. Do you recall that, Mr. Dimitrov?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was number 208 for person from Tripoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You have a very good memory, I see. Mr. Dimitrov, I would like actually to correct myself because the first guest book which starts in March 2002, started with the second methodology, not with the first entry, but one month approximately afterwards. Therefore, for a period of one month, second guest book was still using the first methodology. It was after mid-April until March 2004 that the second methodology was applicable in the second guest book. I just wanted to clarify that with you, Mr. Dimitrov.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that the first methodology was used for sometime and if you say it was sometime in April when we started the second methodology I agree. And it is used up to date.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. Just to have it in the record if we could go quickly to 65 ter 1213, which is actually tab number 10, Mr. Dimitrov. And if we could go to e-court page 33, which should be page 32 in the hard copy, Mr. Dimitrov. As I mentioned you can see in the entry 191 that one person from Santa Patna de Mogoda actually is recorded from the 16th of April until the 17th of April, 2002. If we go to the next page, Mr. Dimitrov, which should be 33 in e-court, 33 in your hard copy you see the same person in the entry, 197, he or she appears registered for the following day. But then as can you see in entry 198, the second methodology starts to apply, as this person from Edinburgh is registered from the 18th of April, until the 27th of April, 2002. So, Mr. Dimitrov, will be fair to say that the authorities required or change the methodology system in order to have a more accurate methodology of recording and also to avoid possible mistakes in the books?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, the organs wanted us to follow the new methodology. The person that you are mentioning here, I'm not sure and at least I cannot confirm today it is possible that the person said he would stay just for one night and then changed his attention to stay for more nights. I really couldn't say. It is the book that gives the information. I am unable to give the correct information right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that after entry 198, you can see that the new methodology applies? You are free to check the following page, if you wish, Mr. Dimitrov.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, madam. I already said maybe that person said that he would stay for just one day, and he was registered for that day and checked out for the following day. Maybe the next person -- the next day the person changed his mind and wanted to stay for longer. Maybe that person wasn't sure how long he would stay in that hotel in the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But, indeed, he or she appears registered for longer than one day, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what I'm say.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. But, Mr. Dimitrov, you didn't answer my first question. I was putting to you whether this changes made by the authorities in the way of recording the entries in the guest books were generally made in order to achieve a more accurate, accurate way of recording the entries and to avoid possible mistakes.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organs, that is the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the department for control of foreigners, they come to us and tell us what methodology we should use. It is not up to us to think whether the new methodology is more accurate than the previous one, or better than the previous one. It is up to us to follow the instructions from the Ministry of Internal Affairs pertaining to the registration of guests.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrov, I will move to another topic now. If I recall from your evidence in chief, you said that in 2001 you had two people working at the reception desk; one lady and also a young gentleman. And they were working in two shifts, like early morning until late afternoon shift and then the other person would start late afternoon until evening, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person -- I apologise. The first person starts his shift at 7.00 in the morning and works until half past 1.00 -- no, sorry, 3.30 p.m., and the second person comes at 3.30 p.m., and leaves at 10.00. And he has additional half an hour to take the card and forms that I mentioned yesterday to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And, in general there will always be the same persons who will work in the same shift, meaning the lady in the mornings and the gentleman in the afternoon and evenings.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very often if not always the lady worked in the morning shift, and the young man worked in the afternoon shift, unless the lady needed some days off, then he would take her shift as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And what about the nights? What about one guest who wants to check into the hotel after 10.00 or 10.30 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the beginning that we are registered as bed and breakfast, not as a hotel. And our obligation is to have a person at the reception desk until 2200 hours. If a person wants to check in or check out after this time, then in the restaurant, because the restaurant covers most of that building, there is a cleaner and there is a night guard. The cleaner is given the keys, in cases when we have a guest that announced his or her arrival after 2200 hours. The night guard takes the person to the bed and breakfast facility, opens the door and reports the guest's arrival to the receptionist in the morning and the receptionist, that is in the morning shift, registers the guest and notes down all information that are required.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks. And, Mr. Dimitrov, correct me please if I understood you wrong in your evidence in chief, I understood that in general, meaning during the day, if a person wants to check in into your hotel, he or -- his or her personal data will be entered first into a piece of paper, I think that you call it a carton box that will be later taken to the police and it will be afterwards that the information from this piece of paper will be entered into the guest book. That's what you testified, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what I said. As regards the person that arrives after all employees, meaning the receptionist, go home, they are requested to give their passports in the morning to the receptionist that works in the morning shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And when, actually, the information which was initially recorded in these piece of paper in this carton box will be transferred into the official guest book that we have seen?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it is done by the person that works in the morning shift, and most frequently it was Snjezana.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. And how often it will be? Would it be every day, would it be after a short period, a longer period of time, that the information will be transferred from the piece of paper to the guest book?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask Snjezana about this. I really couldn't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know, sir, whether, for a certain period of time, it could be that the information was kept in this piece of paper and it was not transferred into the official guest book, right? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My testimony was that the following day, in the morning, the person who worked in the first shift had the obligation to finish these things, meaning to register the guest in the guest book. Whether the receptionist would do that five minutes after his or her arrival at work or an hour, it's not up to me to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, Mr. Dimitrov, indeed, the person working at the reception desk will be using, as a daily record, another document which will be different from the guest book, a contemporaneous document where every day he or she will be entering the data of the new guests, and perhaps also the time of arrival of the new guests and then later on, meaning the following day, this lady had the obligation to introduce it in the guest book, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a guest arrives, and I said that yesterday, when the guest arrives he is checked -- he is -- he gives information on a separate carton form and this information from the form are put in the guest book. That is all I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But this information will be put in the guest book the following day, right, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a guest arrives at midnight or at 2.00 a.m., then the information about his or her arrival is not registered by anybody else but the person that comes to work in the morning shift, and most frequently it was Snjezana.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Dimitrov. But what about a person who comes within the working hours? My question is, this -- the data, the information of this person, will be initially entered in this piece of paper, right, and only afterwards it will be entered into the guest book. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And when it will be that it will be entered into the guest book? If, for example, one person, let's say, checks in 10.00 a.m. in the morning, his or her information is written down in this piece of paper, right, when that information which will be actually transferred into the guest book.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said very well, madam. If a person comes in the hotel at 10.00 a.m., then we have a receptionist that fills in the form and the receptionist immediately registers the guest in the guest book, just like registration in the form. I said persons that arrive later in the evening or after the working hours, the person that works in the morning shift registers these guests that came during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. So would you agree with me, Mr. Dimitrov, that if this person working in the night by any chance makes a mistake and didn't -- didn't tell actually to this lady all the information about one guest, or omits an information, this lady will write down actually the information that he -- that she was told, right, including the mistake, including the omission?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person that works in the night shift, that person, the only thing he does, is to give the room keys to the guest, and that's all. The day after, the morning after, when the receptionist working in the morning shift arrives, he or she takes the passports or the ID documents from the guest and fills in the forms. So there is a belatedness of ten, 12, hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dimitrov, these originals or these pieces of papers that you mentioned, the piece that you actually gave to the police, did you keep copies of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forms, that we give to the ministry of interior affairs we are not obliged to keep copies of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So you actually -- we cannot actually -- we cannot compare, we cannot be sure that all of the information that it's registering these pieces of paper is actually included in the guest book, right, because you are not keeping a copy of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you are saying. I'm not saying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But how can we be sure if we don't have that original piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original document is the passport. It happens very often that the passports or ID cards of the guests are kept and are not given back to them until they leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But you didn't answer my question, sir. I was asking that as you didn't keep actually these original carton, these original pieces of paper that you give to the police or you didn't make copies, you were not in a position to actually compare in 2001 when you were doing like single entries per day, you were not in a position like to check whether the entries were correct against the piece of paper that you had given to the police?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I told you that very often we keep the passports until the guest checks out.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrov, you have testified that you were not the one who were doing the entries, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I have not made any entry yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And you're actually a busy man travelling quite often because of business. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the period that we are talking about, and that was two or three months that the upper floor of the facility was working where the bed and breakfast is, I was really interested in everything. I wanted to know how many rooms were occupied. I wasn't interested in the names of guests.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And, indeed, you were not even in Macedonia from the 6th to the 19th of August, 2001, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 6th to the 19th of August, I was not in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So even if you had wanted, you were not in a position to check whether the record -- the registering of the guests was properly done.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're trying to put to me, but I have to say that I believe that there was no mistake made.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You believe there was no mistake there made. But, again, you were not there to check it, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every man can make mistakes, but I'm convinced that the employees were not trying to make manipulation with the information. I have no such indications at least not until now. As a matter of fact, why would anybody make a mistake for that period, because then mistakes could have been made in the period afterwards, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about manipulation, Mr. Dimitrov. I'm talking about omissions or mistakes basically. You actually have testified that information that was entered in this carton, this piece of paper if it was during the day when the person was at the reception desk was actually transferred straight away into the guest book. But you actually -- that was the instruction that that was instructions that they actually gave to the people in the reception, right? You were not in a position to check that the information was transferred straight away, at the same time, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the person that was giving the instructions to the employees, by the ministry of interior affairs as pertaining to the guest books. At the beginning I said because we were only working for a few months I was checking every day how many rooms were occupied. I wasn't checking the names of the guests.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So you actually -- you know for certain that the transfer of information from that carton from that piece of paper to the book was done at the same time, right, it could happen that it was during the day?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you several times, that if a person arrives late in the evening, his registration is done in the morning after, and that is what I've reiterated several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sir, can we please go to Exhibit P542, which is tab 4 in your binder. And if we could go, please to the first photo. Yes. Sir, this is the first guest book, the one which goes from March-- excuse me, May 2001 until March 2002. Would you agree me -- that is actually the cover. Would you agree with me that the cover page practically looks new in touch from the exterior?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And if we could go please to the next page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is not the case with the second guest book as we can see that the binding is a bit broken as well as the edges are a bit torn? Would you agree with me in this visual observation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go please to the third page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sir, the second guest book is the one which is placed on the top of the photo. As can you see, the pages in the second guest book are a bit more yellowish, and they look a bit much more used than the first one. Would you agree with me on that visual observation, Mr. Dimitrov?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last photo, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Again, sir, we see in the upper part of the photo the second guest book and in the bottom of the photo we see the first and much older in time guest book. We see that the binding of the second guest book is broken, while the first book looks in a good shape. Would you agree with me in that visual observation, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And if we could briefly go to Exhibit 1D331, page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: It will be tab 8 of the binder, sir. Sir, you have been shown this photo in your examination-in-chief, and you -- well, would you agree with me that the piece of paper appears -- the piece of paper actually from the Macedonian authorities appear -- appears a bit broken, right? Actually, the second -- the second guest book is the one which is placed in the upper part of the photo, of the screen, yeah.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that the paper is torn.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You actually testified on page 56 of yesterday's transcript that this slight crack on the stamp of the Macedonian authorities was done by the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, Mr. Thomas Kuehnel, while reviewing the book. But, Mr. Dimitrov, you were not present, were you, when he was actually reviewing the book?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During yesterday's session I did mention that Snjezana conveyed to me that this was done by Mr. Thomas Kuehnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So it is your evidence that Mr. Thomas Kuehnel, in front of Snjezana and together in front also of the interpreter of the Office of the Prosecutor, actually he made this slight crack in the guest book. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that Snjezana told me that Mr. Kuehnel had done this, perhaps unwittingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrov, you gave a statement to Defence counsel in March 2007. It was a statement of eight lines dealing almost exclusively with the guest books of your hotel. You recall that, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You knew that most likely you will come to this Tribunal to give evidence about these guest books at some point, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 30 days ago I begin to grasp the fact that I would be coming here.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But in October 2007, when Thomas Kuehnel came to your hotel asking to see the guest books, you were quite aware of the importance of these documents for the current proceedings, right, you had given a statement about them.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke with Mr. Kuehnel, and I knew what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Knowing that you would most likely come to testify before this Court and to talk mainly about these books, it didn't occur to you to inform your lawyer, the lawyer to whom you gave the statement, even to call Thomas Kuehnel or the Macedonian interpreter, to inform them about what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I knew that I was coming here, this was something I didn't think was going to be discussed until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But, sir, in your statement, in March 2007, you are almost talking only about your guest books, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement of March 2007, I do speak about my guest books.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please call 1D330 and go to page 1. It's a 92 bis attestation of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Dimitrov, I think that in tab 1 you only have your statement, not the 92 bis attestation. But you can look at the screen and you will see that. Sir, in January of this year your statement was certified by a presiding officer of the registry of this Tribunal. In this proceeding in general, the witness, meaning you, is always given the opportunity to amend or to clarify or even to add something that he or she believes important or feels that it is incorrect in his statement. In particular, if we look -- if we could please go to the second page. Sir, you see additional remarks. That's like in the centre of the screen. In general, there it will be when the witness wishes to introduce a modification from his or her statement. But it seems that you didn't introduce any modification, any clarification. Basically in January 2008 you knew that you were going to testify here, and you didn't add this relevant fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the person from the Tribunal came, when I was signing the statement and asked me whether I agreed with the statement I concurred and I said I agreed. My only comment was that I wasn't 100 per cent sure about part 2 or 3, I'm sure exactly which point. As for the issue about certain tears in the book, I really had no idea about this or that I should be thinking about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But, sir, if you actually -- you had expressed your concern about the number of years that the books have to be kept according to the legislation, generally, I mean, it should be added there, it should be added in additional remarks but is not there, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where -- saying to me today. Up until today I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But I'm just putting to you, sir, that if you indeed told the representative of the registry of this Tribunal that you were not sure about certain paragraph of your statement he or she would have entered that concern in that additional remarks part and it's not there.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this, that I wasn't 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if we could please go to -- again, to that the previous photo which we had in the screen, which is in tab 8 of your binder, 1D331, page 8. Sir, you testified -- you have it in front of you, sir? Yeah. Sir, you testified in-chief that this piece of paper and this stamp are given by the Macedonian authorities after you buy the guest book, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once we buy it, once we make the binding, as it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And you testified that the purpose of this piece of paper and this stamp is to guarantee the accuracy and reliability of the book. Do you recall this evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall having said this.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could please go to 65 ter 1214. It's tab 9. And if we could go to page 200 in Macedonian and it's the only page in English which is translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: That's actually the first guest book that it was provided by you to the investigator of this Tribunal. Sir, do you see the date when this stamp was -- and this actually piece of paper was actually placed into the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date is 10th of May, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 3 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: It will be, sir, the first page of the guest book that it still is in tab 9, and it is only in Macedonian. Sir, do you see the date of the first entry of your first customer ever.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date is 23rd of May, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Actually, 13 days after the Macedonian authorities gave you stamp your guest book, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sir, actually, the stamps and the piece -- this piece of paper which is glued into your foreign guest book, they are actually issued at the very beginning when you still didn't even start recording the information in your guest book, right, when basically the guest book is empty?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question well. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sure. When the Macedonian authorities stamped and put the date, 10 of May, 2001, did you have any entry in your guest book? Had you registered any clients?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of the 10th of May, when the stamp was placed there, up until the 23rd of May of the same year, that is to say, 13 days later, this is the first guest whoever came to us. 14 days we had no guests at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So basically your answer is, no, that when the Macedonian authorities actually stamp, when the Macedonian authorities actually stamp and review the guest book, the guest book was empty basically?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the guest book was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to this stamp that we have seen, is there any physical evidence in the guest book which shows us that the Macedonian authorities have checked the content of the book, as well as the accuracy?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physical evidence that the Macedonian authorities from the MOI, there is no -- there is no such evidence. But when they feel there is a need to do so they come and check the book and they take information which they deem to require.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But, sir, in other words you are telling us that in your guest book there is no stamp, there is no evidence that the Macedonian authorities have reviewed the guest book once the guest book has been completed or when the guest book has been filled, right? They didn't sign it, they didn't stamped it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not mine to say how the Macedonian authorities should behave.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could I take your answer as a no?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can take your answer -- my answer in the following manner. When the police come, they look at the guest book, they take the information they need, and they leave. That's it. For me, it is important to make the payment, the daily payments for those guests which are my guests to pay my taxes. The rest is not mine ...

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But there is no evidence that the Macedonian authorities actually came and look at your book, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the Macedonian authorities come to look at the book or not, this is their right. They resort to as much as they feel they need to. For me, it is important that I don't look at the guests by their first or last names. I look at the number of guests which are at the bed and breakfast and the amount of money which needs to be collected.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sir, can you please go to tab 15, which will be Exhibit 1D333. These are the set of bills that you actually brought this weekend and gave to the Defence, the ones regarding the dates 22nd to 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I believe that you testified -- it's in tab 15. Sorry, sir. Tab 15 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 15. I only see an English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Can you work, sir, with a computer, with the screen? Thanks. Sir, you testified that actually this first page was the receipt where the bookkeeper paid to the bank the amount that the customer had paid. Do you see this signature of Mr. Hutsch in this piece of paper, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it. It is not necessary for Mr. Hutsch to have his signature here. When you go to a cafe and you pay in cash, surely you don't sign anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we please go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: It's a bit blur in the screen, sir. This is the computer -- you testified that this is the computer report. Do you see the signature of Mr. Hutsch in here?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hutsch's signature is also not to be found here.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: You testified, sir, that this was the bill. Do you see the signature of Mr. Hutsch in here?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the bill which we had to buy and give at that time. We don't have such bills anymore. And here also we don't have the signature of Mr. Hutsch.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So, sir, we, indeed, cannot be certain that these bills refer to Mr. Hutsch, can we? His signature is not to be seen anywhere.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you are not sure, but I am sure, because this guest came with such an ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm putting to you that the method of recording the entries and departures of the foreign guests in 2001 was unreliable and it was therefore possible that omissions or mistakes might have been made with regards to the entries in the foreign guest book in 2001. Would you agree with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your opinion, madam. Mine is not the same. I have no indications that I have made a mistake anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mettraux, is there any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dimitrov. I have a few question for you. Do you recall that my colleague this afternoon asked you a number of questions about possible mistakes and omission that could be done by the night guard that could, in turn result in mistakes and omission in the recording of the guests. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall also the suggestion that was made by my colleague that you did not, yourself, personally verify the guest book to ensure that the information contained therein was accurate. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you review by any chance your -- the record of your invoices for the month of August of 2001 to see whether any invoices related to Mr. Hutsch?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And aside from the invoice that was just shown to you by my colleague which covered the 22nd to the 31st of August of 2001, was there any other invoice that related to Mr. Hutsch for the month of August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not succeed in finding any other bill for the person Hutsch for the period of August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And just a moment ago my colleague was asking you about steps taken by the police, I think you said the alien police or the foreign police of the Ministry of Interior to verify your guest book. Could you give a general indication as to how often -- how often the foreign or alien police of the MOI would come to your hotel to look into your book?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot interfere how often and when the police will come. They come at their own finding. Sometimes it's two times a week; sometimes it's two times a month; sometimes it is less frequently. It is up to them. I have no influence on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you recall, Mr. Dimitrov, that my colleague asked you a number of questions about the appearance of these two books, the guest books that you have there? Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps as an introductory question, it may be obvious, but do those books get used, get worn out when you use them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, again, perhaps an obvious question, but do they get more used the more you use them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. The more they're used, the more used they became. Same as clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it correct that the first book, the first book that you opened for the bed and breakfast, covered a period of time of approximately nine or nine and a half month from the 23rd of May of 2001 to the 8th of March of 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it correct that by contrast the second book was used for a period of two years or approximately 24 months from the 8th of March of 2002 until the 1st of March of 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. 27th February. Yes, a couple of days difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would it be correct or would it be fair to suggest that a book that has been used for more than twice as long would, all things being equal, be more worn out than the other book? Would that be a fair suggestion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DIMITROV [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're very clearly suggesting in fact something which is evident, something which is used in the period on a daily basis for two years will not be in the same condition as something used for a lesser period of time within one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. Dimitrov.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Dimitrov, that concludes the -- Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies. I forgot to tender a couple of documents during my cross-examination. Could we now after the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will attend with the witness and then return to that. We would like to thank you for your attendance. Your questioning has concluded. You are now able to return to your normal affairs. Thank you. And the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender, I will seek to tender the Law on Movement and Residence of Foreigners, which was Rule 65 ter 1217, which was in tab 13 of your binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The only relevance -- is the only relevance that there was a period prescribed of two years?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was in Article 73 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's clearly in the transcript. I'm just -- I don't quite see why we need the whole law.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I was going to suggest only Article 73 but if you do not believe that the transcript is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that is clear enough in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour, the second document will be Rule 65 ter 1214, which is tab 9. This document, Your Honour, is a full copy of the first guest book that this witness gave to the investigator, Thomas Kuehnel, when he went to see him in Skopje and it covers the whole period from May 2001 and March 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P594, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, tab 10 which is Rule 65 ter 1213 which is a partial copy of the guest book of the hotel. It's a part of the second guest book which goes from March 2002 until June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what is the relevance of that apart from a change in form of entry?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: That was basically the relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And isn't that dealt with enough in the questioning on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think only tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Regue. As I understand it, Ms. Residovic, or Mr. Mettraux, that is the last witness to be called. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. This was the last witness of the Defence of Mr. Boskoski. We also submitted a request for withdrawal three witnesses from the list. We also informed the Chamber about several other issues that we would like to settle before we conclude our evidence list. First --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you move on, I'm concerned about time and Mr. Apostolski. Can you tell me how long you anticipate these matters that you are now turning to will take?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we can finish within this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you would excuse me a moment. Mr. Apostolski, your opening, how long would you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I believe I will need at least an hour and a half for my opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe after the completion of the opening statement we can proceed with our affairs, so that our learned colleague could finish with his opening statement today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski, if we allowed you an hour and a half, are you comfortable that you would finish in that time? It's important for your opening. We don't want to impede you.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, approximately it would take an hour and a half. I couldn't really strictly determine the time that I might need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Ms. Residovic, can you conclude the matters you have in mind in 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. This is a summary of the remaining 92 bis statements that will be given by Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we mention now that you may have leave to remove the three witnesses from your list. And now we turn to Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And perhaps before I engage into the reading of the summaries of the 92 bis, there was a very brief matter which we wanted to bring to the attention of the Chamber and I understand that Mr. Saxon wished to state something to the same matter and I will do that as briefly as I can. Your Honour remember that on the 14th of February the Prosecution responded to an application by the Defense for a motion from the bar table. I believe yesterday or two days ago we were informed by the Prosecution upon a specific request we had directed to them whether or not the Prosecution had subjected or requested that the intercepts which were the subject of this motion to any testing. The Prosecution at that point informed us that they had in fact sent the material for testing to the Dutch forensic laboratory. This information was not contained in the Prosecution response nor was the fact, Your Honour, that contrary to the indication that was given in the Prosecution response had the Defence refused to give the original. Simply to state the matter as clearly and simply as we can, the CD in its original format which we have contained not only the intercept in question but other material which was given to us pursuant to Rule 70. We therefore gave the indication to the Prosecution that unless they would be able to give us an indication that the expert was unable to test the copy of that material as opposed to the original, we would prefer to stay with the original. The Prosecution did not give us an indication that the expert was unable to test the copy. And we've indicated that we are willing to review or reconsider our position should the Prosecution in the meantime tell us that the expert was encountering any difficulty in this testing. We don't have any such indication and this is why our position remained the same, but more importantly, Your Honour, is the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're wanting an expert to test, or the Prosecution is, electronic recordings of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Your Honour, we understand we had indicated to the Prosecution that they have the CD because we made a copy for them at the time and the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is you have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I tell you it doesn't need any great knowledge of technology to know that each copy is less reliable and accurate than the original. Why is the difficulty about having the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The difficulty, Your Honour, was the fact that the original contained other material which we have been provided under Rule 70 and that we did not wish to disclose on that. If we withdrew the material from that particular CD, the CD would not be original. We also understand from our own discussion with the people from the laboratory in The Netherlands here that they are in fact able to test the material in question in its copied format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can test anything. The question is how reliable is the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this particular instance I can only await the results by the forensic institute which we understand will be forthcoming this week. The indication we got in relation to the material and having described to them the specific CD was that they would be indeed able to test it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Mettraux, that you want the Chamber to hold its decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- which is imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Until that time when the Prosecution received the result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Saxon, anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I was going to make the same request, Your Honour, that the Chamber simply hold its decision in abeyance until we receive a report from The Netherlands Forensic Institute, which has been promised to us no later than the 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, you are been successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: For once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, many times, many times, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may, I will now turn to the summaries of the Rule 92 bis statement of the Defence witnesses and I will start with the summary of the statement of Dr. and Excellency Srgjan Kerim. His Excellency Dr. Srgjan Kerim is a citizen of the Republic of Macedonia. In the year 2001, Dr. Kerim served as foreign minister of the Republic of Macedonia and subsequently as ambassador of the Republic to the United Nations. In those capacities he became acquainted with Mr. Boskoski. Dr. Kerim is currently the president of the General Assembly of the United Nations. In his statement, Dr. Kerim describes the strain which the attacks of the NLA put on all state resources and the efforts of the Macedonian government and state institution to perform their duties under and despite those circumstances. Dr. Kerim explained that as minister, Mr. Boskoski inherited institution that were in the process of maturation and reform, thus rendering the functioning of the government responsibilities more challenging and difficult. Dr. Kerim explains and describes the process of integration of members of various ethnic minority into state organs, a process that had started before the beginning of the NLA attacks. The process was also taking place in the Ministry of Interior under the ministership of Mr. Boskoski. Dr. Kerim states that it was the position of the international community at the time that the NLA was a criminal and terrorist organisation. He points out, in particular, that to his knowledge, no one single state member of the United Nations ever suggested at the Security Council or at the General Assembly of the United Nations that an armed conflict was taking place in Macedonia in 2001 or 2002. Nor does he know of any state member of the UN having supported the NLA or the Macedonian authority as parties to an armed conflict. Dr. Kerim outlines that in 2001 the crisis in Macedonia was regarded as a matter of policing and anti-terrorism. Dr. Kerim explains that the purpose of the state organs at the time was to defend the multi-ethnic nature and territorial integrity of the country and to shield this democracy from the attack of the so-called NLA. Dr. Kerim who knew Mr. Boskoski describes him as a man of moral integrity, a man who as a minister sought to fulfil his duties to the best of his abilities and those of his ministry. The next summary, Your Honour, is that of Mr. Slobodan Casulev. Mr. Slobodan Casulev is a Macedonian citizen who over the years served his country as a diplomate, as a Member of Parliament and as foreign minister. Mr. Casulev testifies to the good character of Mr. Boskoski. He also testified to the great challenges that he and Mr. Boskoski as government ministers met in the years 2001 and 2002 to fulfil their mandates and duties. Mr. Casulev commends Mr. Boskoski for his ability to guarantee and oversee internal stability and security through the enforcement of the Ohrid Framework Agreement. This was a pre-condition and the basis for successful return to peaceful civil society in Macedonia. Mr. Casulev testifies to Mr. Boskoski's cooperation with the international community and his efforts to contribute to the implementation of the Ohrid Framework Agreement. Mr. Casulev knows Mr. Boskoski to be free of ethnic prejudice and to be liked and admired as a political figure in Macedonia. He also knows him to be an honest highly ethical man, a loving father, and a loyal friend. The next summary, Your Honour, is that of Mr. Aleksandar Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic is a Croatian citizen and a journalist by profession. He served in his country, Croatia as an ambassador in the Republic of Macedonia from January of 2001 until November of 2005. He knows Mr. Boskoski both as a state official and as a friend. He describes how ambassadors and other state officials would gravitate around Mr. Boskoski and characterises his contact with such persons as open and friendly. Mr. Milosevic knows of Mr. Boskoski to be free of ethnic or political bias and prejudice, as a patriot who sought to use his office to protect the milti-ethnic and democratic nature of his country. Mr. Boskoski talked of his Albanian friends and his hopes that all citizens of the country could regard Macedonia as their common fatherland. Mr. Milosevic describes Mr. Boskoski as a patriot, a man who viewed the multi-ethnic character of his country and his various religious credes as strengths and treasures to be preserved. As a representative of the international community in Macedonia in 2001, Mr. Milosevic did not believe the various justifications advanced by the NLA to legitimise their activities. He also highlights the fact that the international community never supported the changing agenda of the NLA or their claim of institutional discrimination. He points out that the reform that were intended to improve the position of minorities in the country were slowed down by the NLA attacks rather than facilitated. Mr. Milosevic made it clear from that his discussion with the prominent Albanian political leader the reason for the NLA attacks was the perception that the borders of the former Yugoslavia had not yet solidified. He says that NLA attacks were about territory and control over that territory. Mr. Milosevic also knew of Mr. Boskoski's view that all outstanding problems in the republic should be resolved politically, not through violence. He also knows that Mr. Boskoski strived to carry out his duties as minister in accordance with the laws and constitution of his country while trying to satisfy the various demands that the international community placed upon Macedonia at the time. Among the various contributions that Mr. Boskoski made to that process, Mr. Milosevic mentions the efforts made by Mr. Boskoski to implement the process of reform of the police, the peaceful return of those forces to conflict areas, the integration of ethnic minority into the police forces and generally to ensure the implementation of the Ohrid Framework Agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The last summary, Your Honour, is that of Ms. Nevenka Mikac. Ms. Nevenka Mikac is a citizen of the Republic of Macedonia and a friend of the family of Mr. Boskoski. She knows and describes the family of Mr. Boskoski as a closely knit and loving family, and Mr. Boskoski as a father of three. Kate, a law student, Pance a high school student and Phillip, his 13-year-old son and a primary school student. Ms. Mikac described Mr. Boskoski to be free of ethnic or religious prejudice, a man of tolerance and generosity who from the modest background of his family became a successful business man and later a politician. As a minister Mr. Boskoski remained the modest, honest, moral and fair man who Ms. Mikac knew as a friend, a loving father and a husband. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I believe, Your Honour, that we should formally seek to tender those statement at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, the four statements will each be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, statement of witness Kerim will become Exhibit 1D334. Witness statement of Mr. Milosevic will become Exhibit 1D335. Witness statement of Mr. Casulev will become Exhibit 1D336. And the last statement of witness Mikac will become Exhibit 1D337.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are several other issues for which we would request the Chamber to make a decision. You know that yesterday, to the witness Popovski I showed an article from the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and since other articles from this code were entered into evidence, in accordance with your suggestion, we, this part of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, have translated under number 65ter 1D1322, and we would ask that the document that was registered under 1D329 MFI is accepted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 1D329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the testimony of Witness Vesna Dorevska, admitted into evidence was a decision for employment of Goran Mitevski, in UBK. That was signed by minister of the interior affairs Dosta Dimovska. This exhibit was given the number 1D308. At that moment there was no translation. Now we have a translation that was uploaded in the e-court under the number 1D01-0600 and we would seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Ms. Residovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: More accurately the translation will now be added to the existing exhibit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, on several occasions we spoke about the problems with the translation and in reference to a large document which is the exhibit P96, together with the CLSS, there was a revision of the whole document, and the CLSS submitted to the Defence a revised translation that was uploaded under the ID number 1D01-0539, and 1D01-0499. We seek to -- to replace -- we seek that these two translations replace all other draft translations of this document, with the exception of the part of the translation that is number 1D10-0138 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Frankly, it is not clear to me what the substitution would do in every case, because there has been some questioning on earlier translations. So what I would propose is to receive this new translation as the authoritative translation with its own distinct exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Just in this exhibit, P96, we suggest that the official revised CLSS translations are accepted and that they substitute all of the existing translations that were attached to this exhibit with the exception of the part that is registered 1D01-1318, because this was not the revised part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is too confusing for me at this stage, Ms. Residovic. We will receive the whole of the revised translation of exhibit P96 as a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The translation will be admitted as exhibit P96.1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC

And in the end, Your Honours, witness Kristo Zdravkovski, as evidence were accepted exhibits 1D319 and 1D320, which were two large criminal reports that were submitted in Bitola. utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

Subject to what I believe are now three motions, one of which was received yesterday, and to this written motion which we have just indicated should be proceeded with, and to any other motion concerning an outstanding issue of translation, subject to those matters, the Defence of Mr. Boskoski is closed. utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Tarculovski, your Defence is about to be opened by Mr. Apostolski. Thank you, Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Your Honours, Honourable President of the Chamber, learned colleagues from the Prosecution and the Defence of Mr. Boskoski, pursuant to Rule 84 of the Rules, the Defence of Johan Tarculovski is making this opening statement. The goal of this opening statement will be to summarize the case that the Defence of Johan Tarculovski will present before this Chamber. It will also make several conclusions of the cases presented by the Prosecution and the Defence of Ljube Boskoski. Your Honours, the Defence of Johan Tarculovski is privileged to be making the statement after the presentation of both cases, so that it has had at its disposal almost all the facts that will be the basis for a just verdict by the Trial Chamber. The Defence will limit its case just to additionally confirm and corroborate facts that have already been proven in the Prosecution and Boskoski case. Having heard the Prosecution's case, the Defence had serious doubts whether to have a Defence case at all, because it is completely persuaded that the Prosecution has not proven the responsibility of the accused Tarculovski on any of the basis charged in the indictment. Only on the basis of the Prosecution witnesses the Trial Chamber will be able to reach a just verdict, which is to acquit the accused Tarculovski. Notwithstanding, as I have already mentioned we will have a very limited Defence case consisting of eye-witnesses of the events that happened in the village of Ljuboten before and during 12th August, 2001 and one military expert who, during 2001 was the spokesperson of the Macedonian army and is considered as one of the most relevant scholars in the field of military as a whole in Macedonia. I will commence the Defence with opening remarks and a discussion regarding the existence of an armed conflict in the Republic of Macedonia during 2001. Then I will continue with events that occurred in and around the village of Ljuboten between the 10th and 12th of August, 2001, and will finish with the alleged criminal responsibility of the accused Johan Tarculovski. I will begin with the issue of an armed conflict, because this is a jurisdictional pre-condition and because the findings of this Chamber is of historic importance for history and the general public in Macedonia. In order to determine the existence of an armed conflict, the Prosecution has to prove that there was sufficient organisation and structure of armed forces, such that each participating force has the ability to carry out military operations. It is not sufficient for a group to claim to be organised or to give an appearance that it has a degree of organisation. The standard, under international law, is truly a much more demanding one. The Prosecution has not established that the so-called NLA met the standards relevant to international law in this regard. The Prosecution must demonstrate that the intensity of the armed violence rose to a level that exceeds that of mere banditry, common crime, or a disorganised or short-lived insurrection or terrorist activities which are not subject to international humanitarian law. Determination of the intensity of a conflict and the organisation of the parties are factual and legal matters which need to be decided upon in light of particular evidence and on a case-by-case basis. One of the factors for assessing the intensity of the conflict which the Trial Chamber must take into consideration is the seriousness of the attacks, and whether there had been an escalation of armed clashes, the dispersion of the clashes over territory and over a period of time, an increase in the number of government forces and mobilisation and the distribution of weapons among both parties to a conflict, as well as whether the conflict has attracted the attention of the United Nations Security Council and whether a resolution has been passed in this regard. With respect to the organisation of the parties to the conflict, it must be taken into account factors such as the existence of headquarters, designated zones of operation, and the ability to procure, transport, and distribute arms. Your Honours, as it was seen during the Prosecution case and will be proven during the Defence case, the so-called NLA was nothing but a group of terrorists in the eyes of the whole international community. The so-called NLA was a typical terrorist organisation as defined in all world definitions of terrorism. The so-called NLA were a group of criminals that used violence to intimidate Macedonia and its citizens with the goal of achieving their political goals, and that is the creation of a Greater Albania. There has never been a conflict been Albanians and Macedonians. There was only a criminal attempt made by a terrorist armed group to destroy the constitutional order of Macedonia with a view of creating a territory that they would control. We urge the Trial Chamber not to create a fraction that has never existed or existed only in the minds of the so-called NLA and to consider them as a party to an armed conflict, same as the security forces. There is no valid legal precedent that would support the Prosecution case and the world never recognised this events in Macedonia as an armed conflict nor will it start doing this now. Your Honours, the Republic of Macedonia was the only Yugoslav republic that achieved its independent from Yugoslavia in the 1990s through peaceful means, thanks to its wise people and leaders. After the Kosovo crisis in 1999, whereby Macedonia rescued and provided shelter, food, water, medical relief to over 300.000 Kosovo Albanians, some members of the Kosovo Liberation Army that remained jobless decided to use the Kosovo border in order to conduct terrorist attacks against Macedonia so that they destabilized the country, in order to separate the part of Macedonia inhabited by ethnic Albanians and unite this with Kosovo and all with a view to achieving the ultimate goal, the creation of a Greater Albania. As the honourable American diplomate Mr. Christopher Hill once said, I quote: "We spent the 1990s worrying about a Greater Serbia. That's finished. We're going to spend time well into the next century working about a Greater Albania." Macedonia was then and continues to be the country of all Macedonians, regardless of ethnicity. The NLA was the only group that ever opposed this reality. This is what the general secretary of NATO, His Excellency Lord Robertson, said about the NLA as well as the security chief of the European Union, Mr. Javier Solana. I point to Exhibit 2D69. This is also what the British government, through its ambassador, said about the NLA, reflecting the position of the overall international community. If we could now look at video-clip 2D71.
